title: Arrays and pointers: the array name is an address

visuals.title: Element i is *(a + i): move the index and watch
An array in memory and a pointer walking along it

steps.note: Four int boxes are created next to each other. Each int takes 4 bytes, so the addresses go up by 4.
The name a is the address of a[0] (0x1000). p stores that address, so it points at a[0].
*p means 'the box p points to'. This changes a[0].
p moves forward ONE int (4 bytes): from 0x1000 to 0x1004. Now it points at a[1].
p + 2 is two boxes after a[1], that is a[3]. This changes a[3] (the pointer p itself does not move).
You can point p anywhere inside the array. Now it points at the last box.

goal: After this you can explain that an array name is the address of its first element, use a[i] and *(a + i) as the same thing, walk through an array with a pointer, and say why an array name cannot be moved.
warmup: Think of a row of lockers in the university corridor, numbered one after another. If you know where locker 0 is, you can find locker 5 by walking 5 lockers forward. You do not need a separate map for every locker. An array works the same way: the computer only remembers WHERE the first box is, and any other box is found by counting boxes forward from it.
definition: In Week 4 you used a[i] to reach a box of an array. The big idea of this lesson: the name of an array (like a) is the address of its first element, so a means the same as &a[0]. A pointer is a variable that stores an address (Week 9). So you can write int *p = a; and p will point at the first box. Because the boxes sit next to each other, p + 1 is the next box, p + 2 is the one after that, and so on. That is why a[i] and *(a + i) are exactly the same thing: 'start at a, go i boxes forward, look inside'.
howItWorks: Open the memory visual and press Next. First the 4 boxes are created with addresses 0x1000, 0x1004, 0x1008, 0x100C (4 bytes apart, because an int takes 4 bytes). When you write int *p = a; the pointer p stores 0x1000. The computer is clever about adding: p + 1 does NOT add 1 byte, it adds one whole int, so p + 1 is 0x1004. You can also move the pointer with p++ and read with *p. Two forms mean the same thing: a[i] is *(a + i), and &a[i] is a + i (see the syntax block). Now the important DIFFERENCES between an array name and a pointer variable. (1) A pointer is a normal variable: you can change where it points (p++, p = &a[3]). An array name is a fixed address, like the position of locker 0: it cannot be moved, so a++ and a = something are errors. (2) sizeof(a) gives the size of the WHOLE array (5 ints = 20 bytes), but sizeof(p) gives only the size of one address, so you cannot use a pointer to find how many elements the array has. In the examples we never print the real addresses (they change from run to run); we print values, differences like p - a, and comparisons like p == &a[0].
syntax:
int a[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};

int *p = a;        // same as: int *p = &a[0];

// two ways to say the same thing
a[2]               // element at index 2
*(a + 2)           // same element (a is an address, +2 moves 2 boxes)
&a[2]              // address of element 2
a + 2              // same address

*a                 // first element, same as a[0]
p[3]               // a pointer can also use [ ]: same as *(p + 3)

p++;               // OK: p moves to the next box
// a++;            // ERROR: an array name cannot be changed

sizeof(a)          // bytes of the WHOLE array (5 * 4 = 20)
sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])   // number of elements (5)
sizeof(p)          // only the size of one address

sample.title: The array name is the address of the first element

explanation.text: An array of 4 ints. The boxes are next to each other in memory.
a is the address of a[0], so p now points at the first box. No & is needed in front of a.
p == &a[0] compares two addresses. They are equal, so the result is true, printed as 1.
a[2] and *(a + 2) are two spellings of the same element, so 30 is printed twice.
*a is the first element. *(p + 3) starts at the first box and moves 3 boxes forward: a[3].

steps.note: The array a gets 4 boxes side by side: a[0]=10, a[1]=20, a[2]=30, a[3]=40.
The name a means 'address of a[0]', so p now points at the first box.
p == &a[0] is true, and true prints as 1. The array name and &a[0] are the same address.
a[2] and *(a + 2) both reach the third box. Both give 30.
*a is the first element (10). *(p + 3) moves 3 boxes from the start: a[3] = 40.
main ends.

sample.title: Walking along an array with a pointer

explanation.text: p starts at the first element.
sum is the running total, starting at 0.
The loop runs 5 times, once for each element.
*p is the value in the box p points to. Add it to sum.
p++ moves the pointer one int forward, to the next box.
After the loop p is one box past the last element. We only look at the address; we never read *p here.
p - a is a count of elements between the two addresses: 5.

steps.note: Array of 5 boxes.
p starts at the first element.
sum starts at 0.
Round 1: add *p to sum (now 2), then p++ moves the pointer one box forward.
Round 2: add *p to sum (now 6), then p++ moves the pointer one box forward.
Round 3: add *p to sum (now 12), then p++ moves the pointer one box forward.
Round 4: add *p to sum (now 20), then p++ moves the pointer one box forward.
Round 5: add *p to sum (now 30), then p++ moves the pointer one box forward.
The loop is over. 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30.
p - a counts the boxes between the two pointers: 5. Pointer minus pointer is a number of elements, not bytes.

sample.title: sizeof and pointer offsets (exam question)
sample.expectedOutput:
Bytes in a: 20
Elements in a: 5
Same size as p? 0
2 4 5 1

explanation.text: Five ints, so the array takes 5 x 4 = 20 bytes.
a + 1 is the address of a[1], so p points at the number 2.
sizeof(a) is the size of the WHOLE array: 20 bytes.
Dividing the whole size by the size of one element gives the number of elements: 5. This trick works only on the real array, not on a pointer.
sizeof(p) is just the size of an address, which is not the same as 20, so the comparison is false and prints 0.
p points at a[1]. So *p = a[1] = 2, p[2] = a[3] = 4, *(p + 3) = a[4] = 5, and p[-1] = a[0] = 1. A pointer inside an array may be indexed backwards too.

variations.when: Most readable. Use it when you think in terms of 'the i-th element'.
Exactly the same element as a[i]. Shows that a is an address. Do not forget the brackets around a + i.
When you want to walk (p++) through the array or pass the array on. Same as int *p = &a[0];
variations.example: for (int *p = a; p < a + 5; p++) cout << *p;

variations.when: A pointer can be indexed like an array. p[i] means *(p + i), counted from where p points now.

variations.way: Address of an element: &a[i] or a + i
variations.when: When a function or pointer needs the address of one particular box.
Only for a real array in the same function where it is declared. A pointer does not know how long the array is.

mistakes.error: error: lvalue required as increment operand. An array name is a fixed address, so it cannot be moved. Copy it into a pointer variable and move the pointer.
error: cannot convert 'int (*)[3]' to 'int*' in initialization. &a is the address of the WHOLE array, which is a different type. Use a or &a[0].
No compiler error. *a + 2 means (*a) + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12, because * is done before +. Always write the brackets: *(a + 2).

examTips: Write the key sentence in the exam: 'The name of an array is the address of its first element, so a is the same as &a[0].'
a[i] is the same as *(a + i), and &a[i] is the same as a + i. Learn the three-row table by heart.
p + 1 moves one ELEMENT (4 bytes for an int), not one byte. A pointer p moves with p++, but an array name never does.
sizeof(array) is the bytes of the whole array; sizeof(array) / sizeof(array[0]) is the element count. sizeof(pointer) is just the size of an address.
Never print real addresses in an answer; the exam usually asks for values or differences like p - a.
romanSummary: Array ka naam us ke pehle element ka address hota hai, yani a aur &a[0] ek hi cheez hain.
a[i] aur *(a + i) bilkul same hain: a se i boxes aage jao aur andar dekho.
Pointer p = a likh kar hum array ke upar p++ se chal sakte hain, p + 1 ka matlab agla element hota hai (4 bytes aage).
Pointer ko aage peeche kar sakte hain, lekin array ka naam badal nahi sakte: a++ error hai.
sizeof(a) poore array ka size deta hai, lekin sizeof(p) sirf ek address ka size hota hai.

practice.prompt: int a[5]; Which expression is the same as a[3]?
practice.explanation: a is the address of the first box. a + 3 is the address 3 boxes later, and * looks inside it. So *(a + 3) is a[3]. The option *a + 3 would add 3 to the FIRST element.

practice.prompt: After int a[5]; int *p = a; what does p store?
practice.hint: The name a means the address of the first element.
practice.explanation: p holds an address. Since a is the address of a[0], p points at the first element. It does not copy the whole array.

practice.hint: After p++ the pointer is at a[1].
practice.explanation: p++ moves p to a[1] = 6. Then p + 2 is a[3] = 8.

practice.hint: Write down which elements p visits: it jumps 2 boxes each time.
practice.explanation: p visits a[0], a[2] and a[4]: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. After a[4], p += 2 lands exactly on a + 6, so the loop stops.

practice.hint: An array name cannot be moved. What can you move?
practice.explanation: a++ is an error because the array name is a fixed address. Copy it into a pointer p and move p instead.

practice.hint: Which name is the address of the first element?
practice.explanation: *(a + 2) means 'go 2 boxes from the start and look inside', which is a[2] = 15.

practice.prompt: Write the lines that print all 5 elements of int a[5] = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5} separated by spaces, using a pointer p and *p only (no [ ] at all).
practice.hint: Start p at a and move it one box per round.
practice.explanation: p starts at a[0]. Each round prints the box p points to and then p++ moves to the next. The loop runs 5 times.

practice.prompt: int a[10]; int *p = a; Which statement is true?
options: sizeof(a) and sizeof(p) are always equal
sizeof(a) is the size of the whole array, but sizeof(p) is only the size of one address
p can be used but a cannot be used in expressions
a can be changed with a++ but p cannot
practice.answer: sizeof(a) is the size of the whole array, but sizeof(p) is only the size of one address
practice.hint: One of them knows about 10 elements, the other does not.
practice.explanation: The compiler knows a is an array of 10 ints, so sizeof(a) is 40 bytes (with 4-byte ints). A pointer is just an address; it does not remember how many elements follow.

quiz.prompt: The name of an array is...
options: a copy of all its elements
the address of its first element
quiz.answer: the address of its first element
quiz.explanation: The array name stands for the address of the first box, a[0].

quiz.hint: One uses brackets, the other uses the star.
quiz.explanation: Both mean 'go i boxes forward from the start and look inside'.

quiz.prompt: int a[3]; int *p = a; Which line gives an error?
quiz.hint: Which of the two names can move?
quiz.explanation: A pointer variable can move with p++. The array name is a fixed address and cannot be changed.

quiz.prompt: int *p = a; and a is an array of ints. What does p + 1 point to?
quiz.hint: Adding to a pointer counts elements, not bytes.
quiz.explanation: p + 1 moves one whole int (4 bytes), so it points at the next element.

quiz.prompt: int a[5]; Which expression gives the number of elements?
quiz.hint: Whole size divided by the size of one box.
quiz.explanation: sizeof(a) is all the bytes, sizeof(a[0]) is the bytes of one element. The division gives how many elements there are.
